doc.title: Roscoe Mitchell interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2023

chapter: Performing and the idea of free jazz
title: Subbing for Braxton at Willisau and the solo Nonaah
summary: At Willisau he replaced Anthony Braxton and won over a hostile audience with repetition, leading to the solo saxophone piece Nonaah and its wide interval skips.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Well I don’t know about that but I’ll tell you about my experience in Willisau, Switzerland. I was there with the Art Ensemble. We had played a concert. Anthony Braxton could not get there because of something that went wrong with his travel. So Niklaus Troxler, and I don’t know if you have this record, do you?

Well you need to get it you know. It’s the “Nonaah” record you know. Niklaus Troxler asked me if I would play the solo in the place of Anthony. And so like I said, I’d already played with the Art Ensemble. So when I went on the stage to take the stage, you had people that didn’t like that you know. And they had decided that they were going to like shout me down you know. So I just picked one of the repetitions. You know you need to get some of my records you know. And then you can understand more clearly like what I’m talking about and like Chuck Nessa has these recordings you know. You know so they were determined to shout me down you know and so I just got into the repetition of this composition and I started to play it over and over and over and over. And then variate it gradually and so on. Yeah, now I want you to get this record you know, and then maybe you can write me sometime in the future and tell me what you think of it. You know. But I hit this same repetition over and over and over and variating it so slightly and then all different kinds of ways until the audience was solid, and then I went on to finish my solo version of “Nonaah.” You know. “Nonaah” is a piece that you know started out as a projected one of five projected compositions for solo saxophone. What I wanted to do with that piece was to give the impression of the saxophone sounding like more than one instrument. So I used wide interval skips to exploit the registers. I might play something in the low register and then something in the middle register, the high register, the altissimo register — not a line that’s in the scale fashion but in skips and so on.
